what_its_for: Perphenazine is used to treat symptoms of schizophrenia, such as hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there), delusions, and disorganized thinking. It may also be used to control severe nausea and vomiting in adults.
how_to_take: Take perphenazine exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food, but taking it with food or milk may help prevent an upset stomach. Swallow tablets whole with a full glass of water. Do not crush or chew the tablets. Try to take it at the same time each day to help you remember. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, as this can cause withdrawal symptoms.
dosing: Your doctor will set the right dose for you based on your condition and how you respond to the medicine. For schizophrenia, the usual starting dose for adults is 4 to 8 mg taken 3 times a day. For nausea and vomiting, the typical dose is 8 to 16 mg per day, split into smaller doses. Your doctor may slowly adjust your dose. Never take more than your doctor prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store perphenazine tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, light, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it after the expiration date printed on the package. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of unused medicine.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking perphenazine, as it can increase dizziness, drowsiness, and other side effects. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do anything that requires you to be alert until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid getting too hot or overheating, such as in hot weather or saunas, as perphenazine can affect your body's ability to regulate temperature. Avoid standing up too quickly from a sitting or lying position to prevent dizziness and falls. Tell your doctor about all medicines you take, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements, as many medicines can interact with perphenazine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: stiff muscles, high fever, confusion, or sweating (signs of a rare but serious condition called neuroleptic malignant syndrome); uncontrolled movements of your face, tongue, or body (which could be a sign of tardive dyskinesia); severe dizziness or fainting; fast or irregular heartbeat; difficulty breathing or swallowing; yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice); unusual bruising or bleeding; seizures; or signs of serious allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing. Also call your doctor if you feel more depressed, have thoughts of harming yourself, or if your symptoms seem to be getting worse.
when_it_works: Some people may notice improvement in symptoms like nausea within a few hours to days. For mental health symptoms like hallucinations and disorganized thinking, it may take several days to a few weeks before you notice the full benefit. It is important to keep taking perphenazine even if you do not feel better right away. Talk to your doctor if you do not notice any improvement after a few weeks.
special_populations: Older adults: Perphenazine should be used very carefully in elderly patients, especially those with dementia-related conditions, as it may increase the risk of serious side effects including stroke and death. Older adults may also be more sensitive to dizziness and falls. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Babies born to mothers who took this medicine during the third trimester may have movement problems or withdrawal symptoms after birth. Breastfeeding: Perphenazine may pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: The safety and effectiveness of perphenazine in children has not been well established for most uses. Use in children should only be under close medical supervision. Liver or kidney problems: Let your doctor know if you have liver or kidney disease, as your dose may need to be adjusted.
